candidate.blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort — Nutrition and Oral Hydration: assess feeding needs, provide feeding assistance, and educate caregivers about nutrition/feeding behaviors
candidate.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — responsive infant feeding / hunger cues
candidate.educational_objective: Teach parents to respond to early infant hunger cues such as rooting, hand-to-mouth behavior, and lip smacking rather than waiting for crying or relying on rigid schedules.

options.A: I will look for rooting, repeated hand-to-mouth movements, and lip smacking before the baby begins crying
options.B: I will wait for vigorous crying because crying is the earliest and most specific hunger cue
options.C: I should feed only at fixed clock times even when the baby shows clear hunger cues earlier
options.D: Any sucking behavior always means the baby is hungry and needs another feeding

candidate.rationale: AAP guidance supports responsive feeding for most healthy full-term infants. Typical hunger cues include rooting, hand-to-mouth behavior, lip licking/smacking, opening the mouth, increased alertness, and sucking behavior. Crying is a later hunger sign and can also have many non-hunger causes. Sucking is not uniquely specific for hunger because infants may also suck for comfort. Therefore A is the best answer.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Early infant hunger cues include rooting, hand-to-mouth and lip/mouth behaviors, while crying is a late and nonspecific cue.
candidate.source_document_title: How Often and How Much Should Your Baby Eat?
candidate.source_locator: Sections 'How do I know when my baby is hungry?' and 'Hunger cues': responsive feeding for most healthy full-term infants; crying is a late sign; typical cues include rooting, hand-to-mouth behavior, licking lips/opening mouth; sucking may also be for comfort
